title_en: Town Votes to Keep Its Last Bakery
title_ru: Город проголосовал за сохранение последней пекарни
description_ru: Вымышленная новость о том, как жители городка скинулись, чтобы спасти семейную пекарню от закрытия.
text:
The residents of the fictional town of Wexbury Green have voted by a large majority to buy their own bakery, after its owners announced that they intended to close it. The result of the referendum, which was announced late on Thursday evening, means that Pennywhistle's Bakery, the last shop of its kind in the town, will be owned by the community for the first time in its hundred-year history.

The bakery was founded in 1925 by Augustus Pennywhistle, and it has been run by four generations of the family. Its owner, Marjorie Pennywhistle, aged sixty-eight, said in September that she could no longer afford to keep it open. Rents had risen sharply, flour prices had doubled, and a large supermarket, which opened on the edge of town two years ago, had taken away most of her customers. "I cried for a week," she told a local radio station. "Then I decided to stop crying and start baking one last time."

News of the closure spread quickly. Within days, a petition had been signed by more than three thousand people, which is almost half the population of the town. A retired teacher, Bernard Oldcastle, who had been buying his morning loaf from the shop for fifty years, suggested a bolder idea. He proposed that every household should be invited to buy a share in the bakery for fifty pounds, so that it could be run as a cooperative. "If a football club can belong to its fans," he said, "I can't see why a bakery shouldn't belong to its eaters."

The idea was met with doubts. The town council, which had been struggling with its own budget, said that it could not promise any money. A local businessman, Cornelius Fitch, was reported to have warned that bakeries were not charities, and that sentiment alone could not pay the electricity bills. Mr Oldcastle replied that he had never claimed that it would be easy. Volunteers went from door to door, and a weekend fair was organised in the car park, with cake stalls, a raffle and a bake-off judged by the vicar.

The response was far greater than anyone had expected. By the end of October, more than one thousand eight hundred shares had been sold, and an anonymous donor had given an additional ten thousand pounds on the condition that his name was never revealed. It is rumoured in the town that he is a regular customer who comes in every day at seven for a cheese scone, although nobody has been able to prove it. The shareholders have been promised a free birthday cake each year, which may have helped.

The referendum, held on Thursday, asked residents to approve the purchase of the building and the formation of the cooperative. Of the two thousand six hundred people who voted, nearly ninety per cent said yes. Mrs Pennywhistle, who watched the count from a folding chair, was reported to have said nothing for several minutes, and then asked whether somebody could please check the ovens. She has agreed to stay on as head baker for at least two years, and to train two apprentices.

Economists say that the case is part of a wider trend. Across the country, communities have been taking over pubs, shops and post offices, which would otherwise have been lost. A study published this year found that more than ninety per cent of such ventures were still trading after five years, which is a much higher survival rate than for ordinary small businesses. The researchers suggested that customers who own a share are more likely to be loyal, and are also likely to bring along their friends.

The practical details will now have to be settled. A temporary committee, elected by the shareholders, will decide on the opening hours, the prices and the range of products. Several people have asked for gluten-free loaves, and a group of teenagers has proposed a late-night window for hungry students. The old brick oven, which has been burning since 1951, will be inspected by an engineer next week. Mrs Pennywhistle has warned that it is temperamental. 'It likes some people and not others,' she said, 'and it has never liked accountants.'

Not everyone is celebrating. The managers of the new supermarket have declined to comment, although a spokesperson said that the company would continue to offer low prices and a wide choice. Mr Fitch has admitted that he was wrong, and he has bought five shares in the bakery for himself as a gesture of apology. "I'd never been so happy to be proved mistaken," he said, holding a warm cinnamon bun.

Local children have taken part in the celebrations as well. The primary school has decided to design a new logo for the shop, and a competition was held to choose a name for the cooperative's first special loaf. The winner, a seven-year-old girl, suggested the Wexbury Whopper, which the judges described as bold, if a little alarming. It will be on sale every Saturday, and the proceeds will go to the school library.

On Friday morning, the queue outside the shop stretched down the high street and around the corner. The first loaf of the cooperative era was sold to Mr Oldcastle, who ate it standing on the pavement and declared it the best bread he had ever tasted. His fellow shareholders were said to be in complete agreement.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Тот же положение языка, что для θ, но с голосом: звук гудит, не «з».
Перед ударной гласной p, t, k произносите с лёгким придыханием, как маленький выдох.
Ударение ставьте на нужный слог: ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону, остальные сокращаются.
Звонкие согласные на конце слов не оглушайте: «good» не «гут», «world» не «ворлт».

questions.question: Why did the owner want to close the bakery?
questions.answer: Rents and flour prices had risen and a supermarket had taken her customers.

questions.question: What was Bernard Oldcastle's idea?
questions.answer: Every household should buy a share for fifty pounds so the bakery could be run as a cooperative.

questions.question: How did the referendum end?
questions.answer: Nearly ninety per cent voted yes.

questions.question: Why did Mr Fitch buy shares?
questions.answer: He admitted he was wrong and wanted to apologise.
